Thrice
THRISE
adverb
From the Old English thriga / thriwa (three times), which took the Middle English adverbial genitive -s to become thries, then thrice: literally ‘three times.’

Biblical Definition

Thrice is simply ‘three times,’ but in Scripture the number rarely counts idly; it presses toward completeness, solemn confirmation, or hard trial. Our Lord foretold, “before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Mat 26:34), and the threefold denial — matched afterward by a threefold “lovest thou me” — makes Peter’s fall complete and his restoration equally full (Joh 13:38; Joh 21:17). Three times a year all Israel’s males were to appear before the LORD (Exo 34:23), the appointed feasts binding the year to worship. Paul, numbering his sufferings, was “thrice” beaten with rods and “thrice” he suffered shipwreck (2Co 11:25), and thrice besought the Lord about his thorn (2Co 12:8). The word gathers the weight of a thing done to the full: a denial thrice is no slip but a settled failure; a beating thrice is no accident but a pattern of affliction; an appearing thrice a year is a rhythm of covenant devotion. Yet mark the mercy — where sin abounded thrice, grace abounded to restore thrice; where the servant suffered thrice, the Lord’s grace was sufficient. The number that measures Peter’s shame measures also his recommissioning. Thrice teaches that God counts our falls exactly, and answers them with a completeness of grace that overtops the completeness of our sin.

Webster 1828 Definition

Three times; and figuratively, to the full, or with emphasis.

expand to see more

THRICE, adv. [Old English thriga, three times.] Three times.

Used to number a thing done three several times: as, he denied thrice.

By a common idiom, put for completeness or emphasis, as we say thrice-blessed, thrice-happy.

In Scripture it marks solemn repetition — the three yearly feasts, the threefold denial, the thrice-besought petition.

Distinct from a vague ‘often’: it counts exactly, and the exact count carries the meaning.

Key Scripture

Mat 26:34 — "Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, That this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice."

Exo 34:23 — "Thrice in the year shall all your men children appear before the Lord GOD, the God of Israel."

2Co 11:25 — "Thrice was I beaten with rods, once was I stoned, thrice I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I have been in the deep;"

Joh 13:38 — "Jesus answered him, Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake? Verily, verily, I say unto thee, The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice."

Modern Corruption

Not a disputed word but a counted one; ‘thrice’ recovers the exactness with which Scripture numbers both our falls and God’s mercies.

expand to see more

The word rebukes our vagueness about sin. We prefer to say we failed ‘a few times,’ blurring the count; Scripture says Peter denied his Lord thrice, and will not let the number soften. God keeps precise books. Yet the same exactness is our comfort: He who counted the three denials counted also the three restorations, and the servant beaten thrice was upheld by a grace measured to the need. To lose the word is to lose the discipline of naming sin by its true number and mercy by its true measure.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Modern speech simply drops the word for ‘three times,’ a small loss of cadence — but with it can go the biblical habit of exact reckoning. Recover the principle that God numbers precisely: our falls are neither exaggerated nor excused, and His grace answers each by count, restoring Peter as many times as he denied.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

An Old English numeral adverb, thriga, that took the -s of the adverbial genitive and came down to us as thrice.

expand to see more

thriga / thriwa (Old English) — three times; the base numeral three made adverbial.

-s (adverbial genitive) — the same ending that gives once and twice, whence thries, then thrice.

Kin: once, twice, thrice — the old counted adverbs, of which thrice is the last still bearing an archaic ring.

Behind Mat 26:34 the Greek is simply tris — three times — plain in count, heavy in sense.

Scripture’s threes are seldom idle: feast, denial, and petition all use the number for solemn fulness.

Usage

"He denied thrice and was restored thrice: God answers our falls by count."

"Thrice a year Israel appeared before the LORD — devotion has a rhythm."

"Paul besought the Lord thrice, and learned that grace, not removal, was the answer."
